title: Who Saw the Bear?
bodyHtml:
Turkish is the national language of Turkey, spoken by approximately 80 million people in Turkey and elsewhere.

B1. Below are some sentences in Turkish, along with their English translations. Fill in the entries that are missing from the table.

TurkishEnglish
Balık yüzdü.The fish swam.
Zürafa atladı.The giraffe jumped.
Fil koştu.The elephant ran.
Kaplan kaplumbağa için atladı.The tiger jumped for the turtle.1
Balık kaplan gibi yüzdü.The fish swam like the tiger.
Fil ayı gibi yüzdü.The elephant swam like the bear.
Fil atladı.
The turtle ran for the fish.

B2. Here are some more Turkish sentences with English translations. Fill in the entries that are missing from the table.

Kurbağa zürafayı gördü.The frog saw the giraffe.
Zürafa martıyı gördü.The giraffe saw the seagull.
Arı kurbağayı gördü.The bee saw the frog.
Kim martıyı gördü?Who saw the seagull?
Kim arıyı gördü?Who saw the bee?
Arı kimi gördü?Whom did the bee see?
Balina kimi gördü?Whom did the whale see?
Martı kaplumbağayı gördü.
Who saw the bear?
Whom did the bear see?

1. Whenever “for” appears in a translation in this problem, it means “for the benefit of,” not “toward.” (This information is not relevant for solving the problem.)

questions.promptHtml: (b) Turkish for “The turtle ran for the fish.”
(a) English translation of Martı kaplumbağayı gördü.

questions.promptHtml: (c) Turkish for “Whom did the bear see?”

hints.text: Start by lining up the words one by one. In every Turkish sentence here the verb comes last, so whatever sits in front of the verb is doing the grammatical work. Compare where the animal names sit in a one-animal sentence versus a two-animal sentence.

In B1 the extra words için ("for") and gibi ("like") come after the noun they belong with, not before it, and the noun itself is unchanged. In B2 something new happens: the animal that is seen carries an extra ending, while the animal that does the seeing does not. Work out what that ending is and how its vowel is chosen; then notice that the question word behaves exactly like the noun it replaces, taking the same ending when it is the one being seen.

Take a row that is already given: Arı kurbağayı gördü means "The bee saw the frog." The plain word for frog is kurbağa (you can see it in kaplumbağa-style words and in "The bee saw the frog" versus "Kurbağa zürafayı gördü", where kurbağa is the seer and carries nothing). So the object ending here is -yı: a -y- appears because kurbağa ends in a vowel, and the vowel of the ending matches the back, unrounded vowels of the stem. Do the same reasoning for martı in Kim martıyı gördü? and you will have the rule you need.

explanationHtml:
Step 1: find the word order

Look at the simplest sentences in B1:

  • Balık yüzdü. = "The fish swam."
  • Fil koştu. = "The elephant ran."

So balık = fish, fil = elephant, yüzdü = swam, koştu = ran, atladı = jumped. Notice there is no separate word for "the": Turkish simply has no definite article. And the verb comes last.

Step 2: words that come after their noun

Compare:

  • Kaplan kaplumbağa için atladı. = "The tiger jumped for the turtle."
  • Balık kaplan gibi yüzdü. = "The fish swam like the tiger."

English puts "for" and "like" before the noun ("for the turtle"); Turkish puts için and gibi after it (kaplumbağa için). Words like these are called postpositions - prepositions that follow rather than precede. The order in the whole sentence is: subject, then the "for/like" phrase, then the verb.

That gives both B1 answers straight away. Fil atladı. is subject + verb: "The elephant jumped." And "The turtle ran for the fish" is turtle + fish + için + ran: Kaplumbağa balık için koştu.

Step 3: the object ending in B2

Now two animals appear in one sentence, and one of them is being seen. Compare the two rows where kurbağa (frog) appears:

  • Kurbağa zürafayı gördü. = "The frog saw the giraffe." - the frog is the seer, and kurbağa is bare.
  • Arı kurbağayı gördü. = "The bee saw the frog." - now the frog is seen, and it appears as kurbağayı.

So the animal that is seen gets an extra ending. Linguists call this the accusative case: a marker on the noun that says "this one is the object of the verb." English does this only with pronouns ("he" versus "him", "who" versus "whom").

Step 4: what shape does the ending take?

Collect the object forms in the data:

  • zürafa + -yı = zürafayı
  • martı + -yı = martıyı
  • kurbağa + -yı = kurbağayı
  • arı + -yı = arıyı
  • kaplumbağa + -yı = kaplumbağayı
  • kim + -i = kimi

Two things are going on. First, the stems ending in a vowel add a y to keep two vowels apart - arı-y-ı - while kim, which ends in a consonant, needs no y. Second, the vowel of the ending changes to agree with the vowel already in the word: words with a and ı take ı, and kim with its i takes i. This agreement is called vowel harmony, and it runs through the whole of Turkish.

Step 5: the question word

kim means "who / whom," and the crucial point is that it simply stands where the noun it replaces would stand:

  • Kim martıyı gördü? - kim is first, bare, so it is the seer: "Who saw the seagull?"
  • Arı kimi gördü? - kimi is second and carries the object ending, so it is the one seen: "Whom did the bee see?"

Unlike English, Turkish does not move the question word to the front of the sentence or add a helper verb like "did."

Step 6: fill in B2

(a) Martı kaplumbağayı gördü. - martı is bare (the seer), kaplumbağa carries -yı (the one seen): "The seagull saw the turtle."

(b) and (c) both need the word for bear, which appears in B1 in Fil ayı gibi yüzdü. = "The elephant swam like the bear": ayı. For "Who saw the bear?" the bear is the object, so it takes the ending, with y inserted after its final vowel and ı by harmony, and kim stays bare in first position. For "Whom did the bear see?" the bear is the seer, so it stays bare in first position and kim takes the object ending as kimi. The verb gördü stays at the end in both.
